title: Doveweed in Rice Fields: How to Spot Alikbangon and Stop It
metaTitle: Doveweed in Rice: Identification and Control for Farmers
metaDescription: Doveweed, or alikbangon, creeps across rainfed rice fields and grows back from stem pieces. Learn to spot its purple flowers and keep it out of your palay.
excerpt: Doveweed is a creeping broadleaf weed with narrow leaves and small purple flowers. Farmers know it as alikbangon or kulasi. It shows up most in rainfed lowland rice fields, where it spreads by seed and by stem pieces. This page shows you how to spot it between your palay and how to control it before it takes over.

blocks.text:
Doveweed belongs to the dayflower family, Commelinaceae. In the field, people call it alikbangon, kulasi or kulkulasi. Its narrow leaves can make it look like a grass at first. But it is a broadleaf weed, and its soft, branched stems creep along the ground. You will find it mostly in rainfed lowland rice fields, where the soil dries out and gets wet again with the rains.

It is a perennial, so it does not die after one season. It makes seeds, but it also grows from vegetative parts. A stem piece that touches moist soil can root and start a new plant. That is why careless pulling or cutting can leave more plants behind than you started with.

Walk your rice rows and look low, near the soil. This weed has branched stems that creep and spread over the ground. Its leaves are long, narrow and lance shaped, so at first look you may think it is a grass. Even so, it counts as a broadleaf weed, not a grass or a sedge. Check for its small purple flowers on long flowering stems, about 3 to 7 centimeters long. Grasses never carry petals like these, and that is your best clue.

items: Branched stems creeping flat over moist soil between the rice hills.
Long, narrow, lance shaped leaves that can pass for grass at first look.
Small purple flowers on long flowering stems, about 3 to 7 centimeters long.
Patches that grow back from stem pieces after a round of hand weeding.

blocks.text:
This creeping weed takes the same light, water and fertilizer that your palay needs. Its stems spread into low, dense patches between the rice hills. Young rice suffers most, because it is still small and slow to cover the ground.

Since it is a perennial, it does not leave after harvest. Instead, it stays in the field and returns with the next crop. In rainfed fields, the soil dries out between rains, and that gives it room to spread. Thick patches also make hand weeding slower and costlier for your family.

items: When you pull the plants, carry them out of the field. Stem pieces left on wet soil can root and grow again.
Weed early, while the patches are small, before the creeping stems branch and root across the rows.
If you can, keep water in your rainfed field after planting. Fields that dry out between rains give creeping weeds more room to spread.
Pick off plants before the purple flowers set seed, so you block both ways it spreads.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold doveweed down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

items.q: What is doveweed called in Tagalog and other local names?
items.a: Farmers have several names for it. Many call it alikbangon, while others say kulasi or kulkulasi. Its scientific name is Murdannia nudiflora, from the dayflower family. When a neighbor mentions any of these names, they mean the same creeping weed with narrow leaves and small purple flowers in rainfed rice fields.

items.q: How do I control doveweed in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention comes first, so prepare the land well and plant clean seed. Next, hand weed early and remove every pulled plant from the field, since stem pieces can root again. Keep water in the field when you can. If you need a herbicide, pick one by weed group and by the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does alikbangon grow back after I weed it?
items.a: It is a perennial, and it spreads by seeds and by stem pieces. If you chop or pull it and leave the pieces on moist soil, many of them root and grow again. Seeds in the soil also sprout later. So the best habit is to remove the whole plant, carry it out of the field, and check again after a few weeks.
